newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Study sees limited impact from EU cocoa directive.
newsitem.headline: Study sees limited impact from EU cocoa directive.

text.p: The EU directive allowing vegetable fat use in chocolate products will have less impact on the world's cocoa-growing nations than initially feared, the author of a scientific study of the subject said on Monday.
"There is evidence the extent to which cocoa butter will be replaced is lower than originally envisaged," Dr Kees Burger of Amsterdam's Economic and Social Institute told Reuters.
He has just completed a three-month study into the effects of the directive, partly funded by COABISCO, the Association of Chocolate, Biscuit and Confectionery Industries in the EU.

The EU is proposing to allow member states to continue producing chocolate with up to five percent vegetable fat content in a bid to harmonise practices within the trade bloc. The world's cocoa growers have been up in arms over the move, which they fear will drastically cut vital export income.
But the report predicted cocoa butter substitutes would not be fully used in all countries, including the UK and Germany.
"In view of the present use of cocoa butter in countries like Germany and the UK, it is likely that only limited substitution will take place," the report stated.
Assuming France and Italy did not adopt the directive, the reduction in annual bean demand in the EU would be as low as 33,000 tonnes, based on a 13,000-tonne drop in butter offtake.
This amounted to a three percent reduction in demand based on International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) figures, showing EU grindings in 1994/95 of 1.1 million tonnes.
It estimated the maximum amount of substitution at 47,000 tonnes of butter, cutting EU bean demand by 118,000 tonnes.
Some industry estimates have previously put the expected reduction in EU demand as high as 200,000 tonnes.

In addition, the report said the figures must be set against a backdrop of gradually rising prices over the next 15 years and incorporated the formula that for each percentage downward shift in world demand, prices would fall two percent and result in an eventual drop in trade of 0.65 percent.
Thus, one third of the original reduction in demand is recovered but at lower prices.
It considered two scenarios -- one in which prices rose to $2,000 a tonne and one which they rose to $2,800 by the year 2010 from the current $1,400.

"Current outlook for cocoa prices is to go up in the next 10 years by at least 21 percent. The minor shift in EU demand would diminish this growth to 17 percent and the major shift in demand would leave growth of seven percent," it said.

This would cut revenue growth to cocoa producers from the projected 35 percent under unchanged conditions to 30 percent under minimum substitution and to 15 percent under the maximum substitution scenario.
